Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Miguel had spent most of his adult life in uniform, carrying himself with the steady reserve expected of a Navy officer, and until recently he had thought of himself as someone who could stay calm in dangerous circumstances. That belief changed after a deployment that took him through a civilian area in a war zone, where he found himself on the wrong side of an event he still struggled to speak about in sequence. One moment had lingered above the others: the noise, the shouting, the crush of people trying to move at once, and the realization that ordinary civilians were trapped in a situation he could not control. He had been there, close enough to see fear on faces and to hear the panic in voices, and he left with the conviction that he had not done enough. In the months afterward, Miguel kept returning to the same conclusion with a heavy, punishing certainty: he should have protected others and failed, and he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened.

At first he tried to keep the memory contained. He returned to work, remained outwardly composed, and told himself that a man in his position had to carry on. But when the memory surfaced, it did not arrive like a distant recollection. Sometimes it came back with such force that it felt completely real across all his senses at once, as if he were again standing in the same place, hearing the same sounds and feeling the same pressure in the air. He would smell it before he could think about it, and the scene would seem to re-form around him with an immediacy that left him momentarily disoriented. On other occasions the opposite happened: he could remember what had happened, but only in a flat, numb way, as though it had happened to a stranger and not to him. Those were the moments that unsettled him in a different way, because the emotional blankness made him feel detached from his own life, as if the event belonged to someone else while the guilt still belonged entirely to him.

Miguel came to see himself through that event. He had been proud of being reliable, measured, and capable, and now he spoke about himself with a harshness that was new. He had come to believe that he was a weak person, not because others had said so, but because he measured himself against the standard he had set in his mind for what a man, and especially a Navy officer, should have done. He replayed his decisions again and again, each time landing on the same accusations: he had not acted quickly enough, he had not pushed hard enough, he had not protected others when protection had been his responsibility. Even in moments when he was not actively remembering, that judgment sat close to the surface. He would be standing in his kitchen or sitting beside his partner and feel the old sentence rise again — I failed them — followed by the quieter but no less painful certainty that he would never forgive himself for not doing more.

Those reactions began to shape the way he moved through daily life. At work, he continued to report for duty, but the setting that had once given him structure now carried reminders that could pull him back into that memory without warning. Crowded noise, urgent voices, or a sudden commotion in a corridor could make him stiffen and go inward, bracing himself against the force of the recollection. He did not describe dramatic outward scenes; instead, colleagues noticed that he had become more guarded and less willing to linger when conversations turned to operational stories or civilian safety. At home, his relationship had become quieter and more careful around him. His partner could see that some days he was present but emotionally distant, and on other days a single detail — a sound from outside, a chaotic news report, a moment that resembled the conditions around the original event — could leave him visibly shaken and hard to reach for hours. Miguel did not frame his distress as fear in the ordinary sense. He spoke instead of shame and self-condemnation, of being unable to set aside what he believed he ought to have done, and of carrying a sense that his failure had exposed something fundamentally lacking in him.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become difficult to hide. He was no longer able to dismiss the memory as a burden he could simply outlast, and the cycle of vivid reliving, numb recollection, and relentless self-blame had begun to intrude on his work and his life with his partner. What finally brought Miguel to treatment was not a single collapse, but the growing recognition that he was spending more and more of his days bracing for the memory to return and judging himself when it did. He came hoping for relief, though cautiously, and what frightened him most was the possibility that he might be permanently defined by what happened there, forever the man who should have protected others and did not.
